book.subject: cte

title: Site, housing and selecting fattening cattle
competency: Describe site selection, housing, selection criteria and feeds for fattening cattle.

keywords.def: Feeds such as grains, high in protein or carbohydrates.
Feeds such as pasture, hay and silage, high in fibre.
Feed made by controlled fermentation of moist green plants.

en.text: Fattening is most profitable where feed is available locally. Housing must shield cattle from heat and cold, with shade. Choose cattle by age (two to three years is best), sex (steers grow faster than heifers), calm character, good constitution and improved breed.

screens.title: Pick a bull
screens.ask: Which bull is the best choice for fattening?
screens.after: A calm steer of 2–3 years fattens fastest. Read the selection criteria.

screens.title: 3.3.2 Site selection and 3.3.3 Housing
paras: Fattening is most profitable when feed is found locally.
Straw, maize stover, bran and molasses should be in good supply.
Grass must be enough for grazing all year.
Cattle must be shielded from extreme heat or cold. Shade is very necessary.

screens.title: 3.3.4 Selecting fattening cattle
table: Lively but mild, quiet, easy to handle
Big appetite, large heart girth, well-sprung ribs
Improved breeds gain weight faster on less feed

screens.text: What is the preferred age of cattle for fattening?
screens.why: The book prefers two to three years old.
They waste a lot of energy. Calm animals fatten easily.

screens.text: Tap the factors used to select fattening cattle.
screens.why: Age, sex, character, constitution and breed.
screens.clue: Which ones are about the animal itself?

screens.text: Two steers are the same age. One is an improved breed; one is native. Both get the same feed. Which gains weight faster?
screens.why: The book says improved breeds gain weight quicker with less feed than native animals.

en.text: Barley is the best grain for feeding cattle, but wheat, sorghum, maize and oats are also used. Feeds are concentrates (grains, high in protein or carbohydrate) or roughages (pasture, hay, silage, high in fibre). Hay is dried forage; silage is fermented moist forage. Vitamin, mineral and by-product feeds also help.

screens.title: Two kinds of feed
screens.ask: Is dry hay a concentrate or a roughage?
screens.after: Hay is a roughage: high in fibre. Grains are concentrates.

screens.title: Feed and types of feeds
paras: Barley is the best grain for lot feeding cattle.
Wheat, triticale, sorghum, maize and oats are also used.
Oats are used with other grains, not alone.

screens.title: Concentrates and roughages
table: Grains; high in protein or carbohydrates
Pasture, hay, silage; high in fibre
Vitamins and minerals mixed with grains
Left over from processing; often cheap

screens.title: Key words
defs: Feeds such as grains, high in protein or carbohydrates.
Feeds such as pasture, hay and silage, high in fibre.
Feed made by controlled fermentation of moist green plants.

screens.text: Which grain does the book call the best for lot feeding cattle?
screens.why: Barley is best; others are often used too.

screens.title: Sort the feeds
screens.why: Grains are concentrates; pasture, hay and silage are roughages.

screens.text: Hay is forage that has been mowed and dried.
Dawit has teff straw and maize stover, but no grain. What should he add for a balanced fattening ration?
opts: A concentrate such as barley, with vitamin and mineral supplements
screens.ans: A concentrate such as barley, with vitamin and mineral supplements
screens.why: Straw and stover are roughages. A balanced ration also needs concentrates (grains) and supplements.
screens.clue: Which kind of feed is he missing?

items.text: How are cattle selected for fattening? Tap the good choices.
pool: Steers of two to three years
a: Steers of two to three years

test.text: Shade is very necessary for fattening cattle.
test.why: Cattle must be shielded from extreme heat.

test.text: Older animals need a longer time to fatten than younger ones.
test.why: Younger animals need a longer feeding period.
